K2: the cold-start operating requirement for the audit unit
N: How accurate does a count-estimating tool need to be to actually help decisions, compared to just guessing a fixed number, when you have no past results to calibrate it against?
D-sonnet: A named accuracy threshold for a numerical estimate, expressed as a maximum tolerable error size, below which the estimate is worth using instead of skipped. It applies to any situation where someone computes a single number meant to stand in for a count or multiplier that will feed into a downstream judgment, and where the person could instead simply not compute that number at all. The threshold is set on the typical size of the gap between the estimate and the truth, measured on a scale where errors above and below the true value count symmetrically. Below one level of this gap the estimate keeps nearly all of its potential benefit; around a middle level it keeps about half; past a further level the estimate stops helping and instead actively misleads, because a badly wrong number creates false confidence worse than having no number at all. Any specific estimating procedure can be checked against this threshold by measuring its typical error and comparing that figure to the named levels.
D-opus: A stated accuracy threshold that tells you how good a guessed quantity must be before relying on it does more good than harm. It takes as input a measure of how far the guesses tend to land from the truth, and it returns a judgment of how much of the available benefit you keep: small error keeps almost all of it, middling error keeps about half, and large error flips the sign so that using the guess leaves you worse off than falling back on a fixed default number. It asserts that there is a break-even point — an error level past which a guess actively hurts by making you more sure than you should be — and it pins down roughly where that point sits. It applies whenever you are deciding whether a produced estimate is worth using at all, judged against the simpler option of just assuming one standard value. In short, it is the bar an estimate must clear to earn its place.
